phrases.explanation: A prophet would not ask people to treat angels or prophets as lords. The verse again distinguishes reverence for messengers from worship of them. It rejects any religious teaching that replaces devotion to Allah with devotion to created beings.

phrases.translation: Would he ask you to disbelieve after you have submitted
phrases.explanation: A prophet would not tell people to disbelieve after they had submitted to Allah. The passage presents genuine prophecy as calling people toward faith, not away from it. The question invites readers to test religious claims against the consistent message of the prophets.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when Allah made a covenant with the prophets,
phrases.explanation: Allah reminds the prophets of a covenant made with them. The passage stresses continuity across revelation: each messenger’s mission belongs to a shared call to worship Allah and follow guidance. It frames later messengers as part of that prophetic history, not rivals to it.

phrases.translation: ˹saying,˺ “Now that I have given you the Book and wisdom, if there comes to you a messenger confirming what you have, you must believe in him and support him.”
phrases.explanation: If a messenger comes confirming the revelation already given, the prophets must believe in and support him. The condition is confirmation, not contradiction. The verse presents loyalty to truth as more important than status or attachment to one’s own community.

phrases.translation: He added, “Do you affirm this covenant and accept this commitment?”
phrases.explanation: Allah asks the prophets to affirm the covenant and accept its serious responsibility. The question makes their commitment explicit rather than assumed. Prophethood carries accountability: receiving revelation entails recognizing and supporting the truth when it appears.

phrases.translation: They said, “Yes, we do.”
phrases.explanation: The prophets answer that they accept the covenant. Their response models readiness to follow Allah’s guidance, including when it is delivered through another messenger. The verse portrays the prophetic mission as united in its source and purpose.

phrases.translation: Allah said, “Then bear witness,
phrases.explanation: Allah commands them to bear witness to their commitment. Testimony makes the covenant public and binding, not a private intention that can be forgotten when circumstances change. The verse emphasizes integrity in promises made before Allah.

phrases.translation: and I too am a Witness.”
phrases.explanation: Allah also testifies, underscoring that nothing about the covenant is hidden from Him. The next verse warns against turning away after such a clear commitment. The passage therefore links knowledge of revelation with responsibility to respond to it.

phrases.translation: Whoever turns back after this, they will be the rebellious
phrases.explanation: Those who turn back after accepting the covenant are described as rebellious. The verse warns against knowingly abandoning a commitment to truth. Read in context, it speaks of defiance after clear guidance, not of sincere questions or a person seeking understanding.

phrases.translation: Do they desire a way other than Allah’s—
phrases.explanation: The verse asks whether people seek a way other than Allah’s. It frames this question with the reality that all creation belongs to Him. Human beings may still choose their actions, but they cannot escape their dependence on the Creator.

phrases.translation: knowing that all those in the heavens and the earth submit to His Will, willingly or unwillingly,
phrases.explanation: Everything in the heavens and earth submits to Allah willingly or unwillingly. The wording includes chosen devotion as well as the created order’s dependence on divine laws. It does not erase human responsibility for choices made knowingly.

phrases.translation: and to Him they will ˹all˺ be returned
phrases.explanation: All will return to Allah. The reminder of return places earthly arguments and loyalties within a larger horizon of accountability. It invites people to choose guidance with awareness that life ultimately leads back to its Creator.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “We believe in Allah and what has been revealed to us and what was revealed to Abraham,
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to affirm belief in Allah and the revelation given to him, as well as what was revealed to Abraham. Faith is not presented as starting with one community alone. The verse links the Qur’anic message to earlier revelation.

phrases.translation: Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and his descendants;
phrases.explanation: The list includes Ishmael, Isaac, Jacob, and Jacob’s descendants. It recognizes the many prophets and communities through whom guidance came. The verse calls readers to honor this shared history rather than claim that divine revelation belongs to only one people.

phrases.translation: and what was given to Moses, Jesus, and other prophets from their Lord—
phrases.explanation: Moses, Jesus, and other prophets are included as recipients of revelation from their Lord. Their different communities and laws do not make the source of their guidance different. The verse places all messengers within one history of divine teaching.

phrases.translation: we make no distinction between any of them,
phrases.explanation: Believers are instructed not to reject some prophets while accepting others. This means affirming the truth of their prophetic missions. It does not claim that every prophet had identical circumstances or rank. The passage rejects selective belief based on group preference.

phrases.translation: and to Him we ˹fully˺ submit.”
phrases.explanation: The statement ends with full submission to Allah. Belief in earlier messengers is joined to devotion to the One who sent them. The verse summarizes a faith that respects the continuity of revelation while taking its direction from Allah.

phrases.translation: Whoever seeks a way other than Islam,
phrases.explanation: The verse says that a way other than Islam will not be accepted. Here Islam carries the sense of submission to Allah and refers to the revealed path of devotion. The statement follows the affirmation of all prophets and their common call to submit to God.

phrases.translation: it will never be accepted from them,
phrases.explanation: The verse makes acceptance with Allah the central concern, rather than outward affiliation or social advantage. Its claim belongs to the passage’s theological account of submission and revelation. It is not permission for people to coerce another person’s belief.

phrases.translation: and in the Hereafter they will be among the losers
phrases.explanation: Those who reject this path are described as losers in the Hereafter. The warning concerns ultimate accountability before Allah, not a human license to punish or demean others. The next verses speak of rejection after clear proofs and also distinguish those who repent.

phrases.translation: How will Allah guide a people who chose to disbelieve after they had believed,
phrases.explanation: The verse asks how a people could be guided after choosing disbelief despite having believed. The sequence describes a knowing reversal, not someone who never understood the message. Its question highlights the seriousness of turning away after receiving guidance.

phrases.translation: acknowledged the Messenger to be true, and received clear proofs?
phrases.explanation: They had acknowledged the Messenger and received clear proofs, the verse says. Knowledge and recognition make the rejection described here deliberate. The passage speaks about this specific pattern of defiance rather than every person who has doubts.

phrases.translation: For Allah does not guide the wrongdoing people
phrases.explanation: Allah does not guide wrongdoing people who persist in injustice. The statement describes the consequence of choosing wrongdoing over truth. The next verses warn of judgment, while verse 89 immediately affirms forgiveness for those who repent and mend their ways.

phrases.translation: Their reward is that they will be condemned by Allah, the angels, and all of humanity
phrases.explanation: The verse describes condemnation by Allah, the angels, and humanity as the consequence of the defiant rejection just mentioned. Its language conveys the gravity of wrongdoing before the whole creation. It is a statement about divine judgment, not a command for people to condemn individuals.

phrases.translation: They will be in Hell forever.
phrases.explanation: The passage describes a lasting punishment for those who persist in the rejection under discussion. Its severe language warns against knowingly turning away after clear proofs. The following verse makes clear that sincere repentance and reform are met with Allah’s mercy.

phrases.translation: Their punishment will not be lightened,
phrases.explanation: Their punishment will not be lightened, emphasizing the seriousness of the consequence described. The verse warns against treating deliberate wrongdoing as trivial. Human beings should take the warning as a reason for reflection, not as grounds to claim knowledge of another person’s final fate.

phrases.translation: nor will they be delayed ˹from it˺
phrases.explanation: Nor will they be delayed from the punishment, the verse says. The image is one of unavoidable accountability. Read alongside the next verse, it is a warning against persistent defiance, while repentance remains open to those who turn back and change their conduct.

phrases.translation: As for those who repent afterwards
phrases.explanation: The passage turns immediately to those who repent after their rejection. This change of direction matters: the prior warnings do not make Allah’s mercy inaccessible. Turning back to Allah remains possible while a person is alive and able to amend their course.

phrases.translation: and mend their ways,
phrases.explanation: Repentance is joined with reform, meaning a sincere return should be reflected in changed conduct. Merely saying the words while continuing the same wrongdoing is not the full picture presented here. The verse offers hope without treating accountability lightly.

phrases.translation: then surely Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: Allah is All-Forgiving and Most Merciful. The closing assures those who return that their past does not place them beyond mercy. The next verse contrasts this with people who continue to deepen their rejection rather than sincerely repent.

phrases.translation: Indeed, those who disbelieve after having believed
phrases.explanation: The verse describes people who reject faith after previously believing and then continue increasing in disbelief. Its focus is persistence and escalation, not a moment of confusion followed by a sincere return. This follows the promise of forgiveness for those who repent and reform.

phrases.translation: then increase in disbelief, their repentance will never be accepted.
phrases.explanation: Their repentance will not be accepted in the condition described, as they continue deeper into rejection. This should be read with the preceding promise of mercy for genuine repentance, not as a declaration that Allah refuses everyone who has ever doubted or sinned.

phrases.translation: It is they who are astray
phrases.explanation: The verse calls such people astray. In context, it is a warning about continuing to turn from guidance after recognizing it. The passage does not authorize readers to decide who is sincere or to close the door of repentance for others.

phrases.translation: Indeed, if each of those who disbelieve then die as disbelievers were to offer a ransom of enough gold to fill the whole world,
phrases.explanation: Even an amount of gold large enough to fill the whole world could not serve as a ransom for someone who dies rejecting faith. The image shows that material wealth cannot purchase escape from accountability. What matters cannot be replaced by a late payment.

phrases.translation: it would never be accepted from them. It is they who will suffer a painful punishment,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes a painful punishment for those who die in disbelief. Its condition is explicit: it concerns death in that state, not a person who later turns back. The warning calls people to take faith and moral responsibility seriously during life.

phrases.translation: and they will have no helpers
phrases.explanation: They will have no helpers, the verse concludes. No one can overrule Allah’s judgment or substitute for a person’s own response to guidance. The next verse shifts to a practical sign of righteousness: giving from what one truly values.

phrases.translation: You will never achieve righteousness until you donate some of what you cherish.
phrases.explanation: Righteousness is connected with giving from what one genuinely values, not only what is unwanted or left over. The verse invites generosity that costs something and loosens attachment to possessions. It does not prescribe a fixed amount here. It asks for sincere giving.

phrases.translation: And whatever you give is certainly well known to Allah
phrases.explanation: Allah knows whatever people give. The statement assures that generosity is never overlooked, even when others do not see it. The verse connects inward devotion with tangible care for others and introduces an example of generosity in the next passage.

phrases.translation: All food was lawful for the children of Israel, except what Israel made unlawful for himself before the Torah was revealed.
phrases.explanation: The verse says that food was lawful for the Children of Israel except what Jacob had forbidden for himself before the Torah was revealed. It distinguishes an earlier personal restriction from later revealed law. The text does not explain the reason for Jacob’s choice here.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Bring the Torah and read it, if your claims are true.”
phrases.explanation: The People of the Book are challenged to bring the Torah and read it as evidence for their claims. The request grounds debate in a source both sides recognize. It encourages verification rather than relying on inherited assertions or unsupported arguments.

phrases.translation: Then whoever still fabricates lies about Allah, they will be the ˹true˺ wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: Anyone who continues inventing lies about Allah is called a wrongdoer. The verse draws a clear line between a genuine disagreement and knowingly fabricating a claim in God’s name. Its standard applies to every speaker, whatever community they belong to.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “Allah has declared the truth.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to proclaim that Allah has declared the truth. The preceding challenge about the Torah gives the audience an opportunity to examine the evidence. The verse then directs them toward Abraham’s upright monotheism as the proper path.

phrases.translation: So follow the Way of Abraham, the upright—
phrases.explanation: Abraham is described as upright, committed to Allah alone. The Arabic idea of hanif carries the sense of turning away from false worship toward pure devotion. The verse continues the argument that Abraham should not be claimed as a polytheist or defined by later labels.

phrases.translation: who was not a polytheist.”
phrases.explanation: Abraham was not a polytheist, the statement concludes. His example supports the chapter’s emphasis on the one God and the shared mission of the prophets. The following verse identifies the sanctuary associated with worship of Allah.

phrases.translation: Surely the first House ˹of worship˺ established for humanity is the one at Bakkah—
phrases.explanation: The first House established for humanity is identified as the one at Bakkah, another name associated with Mecca. Muslims understand this as the Kaaba, the sanctuary toward which they pray and to which pilgrimage is made. The verse gives the site significance beyond one locality.

phrases.translation: a blessed sanctuary and a guide for ˹all˺ people
phrases.explanation: The sanctuary is blessed and a guide for all people. Its guidance is expressed through worship, prayer, and pilgrimage, bringing people toward devotion to Allah. The next verse points to signs within it and explains that pilgrimage is required only of those able.

phrases.translation: In it are clear signs and the standing-place of Abraham.
phrases.explanation: Among the clear signs at the sanctuary is the standing-place associated with Abraham. The verse links the pilgrimage site to the prophetic history described earlier. It invites reflection on the place’s religious meaning, rather than treating it as a monument alone.

phrases.translation: Whoever enters it should be safe.
phrases.explanation: The sanctuary is described as a place of safety for whoever enters it. This sacred character imposes a duty of respect and protection. The statement is about the sanctuary’s status and should not be used to deny the real-world complexities of safety and access.

phrases.translation: Pilgrimage to this House is an obligation by Allah upon whoever is able among the people.
phrases.explanation: Pilgrimage is an obligation for those who are able. The qualification recognizes that capacity matters, so the duty is not framed as an identical burden regardless of a person’s circumstances. Hajj is an act of worship offered by people, not a need of Allah.

phrases.translation: And whoever disbelieves, then surely Allah is not in need of ˹any of His˺ creation
phrases.explanation: Whoever disbelieves should know that Allah has no need of creation. Worship does not add to Allah’s power or diminish if people refuse it. The verse closes by distinguishing divine self-sufficiency from the human benefit and guidance that worship provides.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “O People of the Book!
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is instructed to address the People of the Book directly. The question that follows concerns rejecting Allah’s revelations, continuing the chapter’s challenge to respond honestly to known evidence. This is a call to account, not an accusation against every individual.

phrases.translation: Why do you deny the revelations of Allah, when Allah is a Witness to what you do?”
phrases.explanation: Allah witnesses what people do, including actions that others may not see. The reminder places the debate under divine knowledge and accountability. It asks the audience to consider conduct as well as public religious claims.

phrases.translation: Say, “O People of the Book! Why do you turn the believers away from the Way of Allah—
phrases.explanation: The verse challenges those who try to turn believers away from Allah’s way. It speaks of a group and a deliberate effort, not of every person who received earlier scripture. Its warning concerns actively obstructing another community’s faith.

phrases.translation: striving to make it ˹appear˺ crooked, while you are witnesses ˹to its truth˺?
phrases.explanation: The effort aims to make the path appear crooked even while its truth is recognized. The verse condemns deliberate distortion and obstruction. It calls for honesty rather than manipulating how others see the guidance.

phrases.translation: And Allah is never unaware of what you do.”
phrases.explanation: Allah is never unaware of what they do. The assurance that wrongdoing is seen offers accountability to those who obstruct guidance and reassurance to those facing pressure. The next verse warns believers not to surrender their faith to such influence.

phrases.translation: O believers! If you were to yield to a group of those who were given the Scripture, they would turn you back from belief to disbelief
phrases.explanation: Believers are warned that yielding to a particular group could turn them away from faith. The verse urges them to guard their convictions against pressure and misinformation, while the surrounding passage concerns deliberate attempts to mislead. It refers to a group, not all People of the Scripture, and does not forbid respectful discussion or peaceful relations.

phrases.translation: How can you disbelieve when Allah’s revelations
phrases.explanation: The audience is asked how it could disbelieve while Allah’s revelations are being recited. The question points to the guidance already available to them. It encourages reflection on what they have heard rather than treating faith as an inherited label.

phrases.translation: are recited to you and His Messenger is in your midst?
phrases.explanation: The Messenger is present among them, so the call is immediate and embodied in a living teacher. The verse recalls the unusual clarity of that moment. For later readers, it underscores the importance of responding sincerely to guidance when it reaches them.

phrases.translation: Whoever holds firmly to Allah is surely guided to the Straight Path
phrases.explanation: Whoever holds firmly to Allah is guided to the Straight Path. The image of holding fast suggests trust and steadfast reliance, especially amid social pressure. The verse turns from challenge to reassurance: guidance comes through taking refuge in Allah.

phrases.translation: O believers! Be mindful of Allah in the way He deserves,
phrases.explanation: Believers are urged to be mindful of Allah as fully as they can. The command calls for reverence, obedience, and awareness in daily life, not a claim that humans can match Allah’s greatness. Taqwa means keeping accountability before Allah in view.

phrases.translation: and do not die except in ˹a state of full˺ submission ˹to Him˺
phrases.explanation: They are told not to die except in submission to Him. This means remaining faithful throughout life, since no one chooses the moment of death. The verse calls for a steady commitment to Allah, not a last-minute performance or despair about human weakness.

phrases.translation: And hold firmly to the rope of Allah
phrases.explanation: The “rope of Allah” is an image for holding to the guidance and bond Allah provides. The verse calls the community to keep that shared connection firmly, especially when disagreement threatens to pull people apart.

phrases.translation: and do not be divided.
phrases.explanation: Believers are told not to divide into hostile factions. This does not forbid every difference of opinion. It warns against division that destroys solidarity and shared commitment. The next phrases recall how Allah brought former enemies together.

phrases.translation: Remember Allah’s favour upon you when you were enemies,
phrases.explanation: The audience is asked to remember its earlier enmity. Recalling that past makes reconciliation a sign of divine favor rather than something to take for granted. The verse invites gratitude for bonds that were not always present.

phrases.translation: then He united your hearts, so you—by His grace—became brothers.
phrases.explanation: Allah united their hearts, and they became brothers through His grace. The change shows that reconciliation can overcome deep social divisions. Their unity is presented as a gift to nurture, not as proof that believers will never disagree.

phrases.translation: And you were at the brink of a fiery pit and He saved you from it.
phrases.explanation: The image of standing at the edge of a fiery pit recalls a grave danger from which Allah saved them. In context, it evokes both the peril of their former hostility and the consequences of wrongdoing. Their deliverance calls for gratitude and care.

phrases.translation: This is how Allah makes His revelations clear to you, so that you may be ˹rightly˺ guided
phrases.explanation: Allah makes His revelations clear so people may be guided. The reminder links communal unity with revealed instruction. Lasting reconciliation is not merely emotional goodwill. It is sustained by returning to guidance and seeking what is right together.

phrases.translation: Let there be a group among you who call ˹others˺ to goodness,
phrases.explanation: The community is told to have a group that calls others toward goodness. The task requires inviting people to what benefits them, not simply criticizing them. Naming a group recognizes that guidance and public service need deliberate effort.

phrases.translation: encourage what is good,
phrases.explanation: The group is also to encourage what is good. This involves supporting constructive actions and helping them flourish in society. The verse pairs invitation with practical encouragement, rather than reducing religious responsibility to disapproval.

phrases.translation: and forbid what is evil—it is they who will be successful
phrases.explanation: They must also discourage evil, with the aim of protecting people from harm and injustice. The verse describes a shared moral responsibility, which should be exercised with knowledge, justice, and care. Success is tied to service, not control over others.

phrases.translation: And do not be like those who split ˹into sects˺ and differed
phrases.explanation: Believers are warned not to repeat the pattern of communities that split and fell into lasting disagreement. The concern is not every sincere debate, but division that hardens after truth has been made clear. The passage has just called for unity and collective moral work.

phrases.translation: after clear proofs had come to them.
phrases.explanation: The warning is especially serious because those communities had received clear proofs before dividing. Knowledge brings responsibility to seek reconciliation and truth. The verse asks believers not to turn evidence into a reason for factional pride.

phrases.translation: It is they who will suffer a tremendous punishment
phrases.explanation: Those who follow this destructive pattern face a tremendous punishment. The statement warns about the spiritual cost of division after clarity. It is not a license to silence sincere disagreement, but a call to keep disputes from becoming injustice and estrangement.

phrases.translation: On that Day some faces will be bright while others gloomy.
phrases.explanation: On the Day of Judgment, faces are described as bright or gloomy, an outward image of contrasting outcomes. The verse moves from community life to ultimate accountability. It invites readers to consider what their choices will mean when they stand before Allah.

phrases.translation: To the gloomy-faced it will be said, “Did you disbelieve after having believed?
phrases.explanation: Those with gloomy faces are asked whether they disbelieved after believing. The question describes rejection after faith, connecting the scene to the earlier warning about turning away from clear proofs. It is a judgment scene, not a verdict people may impose on one another.

phrases.translation: So taste the punishment for your disbelief.”
phrases.explanation: They are told to taste the punishment for their disbelief. The language conveys the seriousness of the choice described. The next verse presents the contrasting outcome for those welcomed into Allah’s mercy, completing the image of two destinations.

phrases.translation: As for the bright-faced, they will be in Allah’s mercy,
phrases.explanation: Bright-faced people are welcomed into Allah’s mercy. Their hope rests not on worldly status but on divine compassion. The contrast with the previous verse emphasizes that a person’s ultimate outcome is determined by Allah’s just judgment.

phrases.translation: where they will remain forever
phrases.explanation: They will remain in that mercy forever. The verse offers a lasting promise of safety and favor. Together, these two outcomes encourage believers to pursue guidance while leaving final judgment to Allah, who knows each person fully.

phrases.translation: These are Allah’s revelations We recite to you ˹O Prophet˺ in truth.
phrases.explanation: The revelations are recited to the Prophet in truth. The verse presents the Qur’anic account as truthful guidance, not a tale adjusted to flatter one group. It calls readers to approach revelation seriously and consider the moral claims it makes.

phrases.translation: And Allah desires no injustice to ˹His˺ creation
phrases.explanation: Allah desires no injustice for creation. The preceding judgment is therefore not arbitrary or oppressive. The verse assures that Allah’s decisions are free of wrongdoing, even when human beings cannot see the full measure of wisdom behind them.

phrases.translation: To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.
phrases.explanation: Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah. The statement grounds divine authority in ownership of all creation, rather than power seized from others. It also reminds people that possessions and positions are entrusted, not ultimately theirs.

phrases.translation: And to Allah ˹all˺ matters will be returned ˹for judgment˺
phrases.explanation: All matters return to Allah for judgment. The reminder follows the description of the Day and places every human decision within a final reckoning. It encourages humility and accountability, since no private or public matter remains outside divine knowledge.

phrases.translation: You are the best community ever raised for humanity—
phrases.explanation: The community is described as raised for the good of humanity. This distinction is tied to responsibility, not unconditional superiority. The actions named next explain what makes the community beneficial: encouraging good, resisting evil, and believing in Allah.

phrases.translation: you encourage good, forbid evil, and believe in Allah.
phrases.explanation: The verse identifies three responsibilities: encourage good, forbid evil, and believe in Allah. Its praise is conditional on ethical conduct and faith, not ancestry or a guarantee that every member behaves well. It then acknowledges that the People of the Book are not all the same.

phrases.translation: Had the People of the Book believed, it would have been better for them. Some of them are faithful,
phrases.explanation: Some among the People of the Book are faithful, the verse explicitly says. This qualification prevents a blanket judgment of the whole community. The passage recognizes sincere believers even while criticizing those who act rebelliously.

phrases.translation: but most are rebellious
phrases.explanation: Most are described here as rebellious, in the passage’s account of those addressed. The statement concerns conduct and response to guidance, not an inherent trait of every individual. The following verses continue this discussion of hostile actions and then affirm exceptions.

phrases.translation: They can never inflict harm on you, except a little annoyance.
phrases.explanation: The verse reassures believers that the hostile group discussed in this passage can cause only limited harm. The wording is tied to that particular conflict, not a statement about every person of another faith. It offers steadiness amid pressure and hostility.

phrases.translation: But if they meet you in battle,
phrases.explanation: The verse then refers specifically to meeting in battle. This is a description of an armed conflict, not a general instruction to fight people of another religion. Its setting matters when reading the claim that follows.

phrases.translation: they will flee and they will have no helpers
phrases.explanation: The hostile opponents are said to flee and have no helpers. The passage describes the outcome of a particular confrontation and presents Allah as the source of protection. It should not be generalized into a forecast about all communities or conflicts.

phrases.translation: They will be stricken with disgrace wherever they go, unless they are protected by a covenant with Allah or a treaty with the people.
phrases.explanation: The verse describes disgrace except where a covenant with Allah or a treaty with people provides protection. The reference to a treaty recognizes that public agreements can safeguard a community. The passage concerns a historical conflict and its specific parties.

phrases.translation: They have invited the displeasure of Allah and have been branded with misery for rejecting Allah’s revelations and murdering ˹His˺ prophets unjustly.
phrases.explanation: The passage identifies rejecting revelations and murdering prophets unjustly as the reasons for the judgment it describes. These are grave acts attributed to the group under discussion, not a claim about every Jew or later community. Verse 113 immediately clarifies that the People of the Book are not all alike.

phrases.translation: This is ˹a fair reward˺ for their disobedience and violations
phrases.explanation: The verse concludes that the described consequences follow from disobedience and violations. Its focus is on actions and broken obligations, not inherited identity. The next verse expressly recognizes upright members of the People of the Book, so the criticism must be read with that qualification.

phrases.translation: Yet they are not all alike:
phrases.explanation: The verse directly corrects any impression that every member of the People of the Book is the same. It introduces upright people among them. This qualification is essential to the passage’s fairness and cautions against turning criticism of a group into prejudice against individuals.

phrases.translation: there are some among the People of the Book who are upright,
phrases.explanation: Some are described as upright, meaning sincere and steady in devotion. Their goodness is recognized regardless of community background. The passage measures people by their conduct and faith rather than treating a whole population as one moral unit.

phrases.translation: who recite Allah’s revelations throughout the night,
phrases.explanation: They recite Allah’s revelations during the night and prostrate in prayer. The description portrays worship as regular and humble, not merely an identity or claim. Night prayer reflects devotion when public recognition is not the purpose.

phrases.translation: prostrating ˹in prayer˺
phrases.explanation: Their worship culminates in prostration, a physical expression of humility before Allah. The passage portrays uprightness through both belief and practice. Its recognition of these people prepares the next verse to describe their faith and eagerness to do good.

phrases.translation: They believe in Allah and the Last Day,
phrases.explanation: These upright people believe in Allah and the Last Day. Their faith includes accountability beyond this life, which shapes how they live now. The verse recognizes shared devotion to God and judgment across communal boundaries.

phrases.translation: encourage good and forbid evil,
phrases.explanation: They encourage what is good and forbid evil, showing that their belief has a social expression. The passage presents moral action as part of righteousness. Their efforts are described positively, not dismissed because they belong to another scriptural community.

phrases.translation: and race with one another in doing good. They are ˹truly˺ among the righteous
phrases.explanation: They compete in doing good and are counted among the righteous. The phrase suggests eagerness to serve, not rivalry for status. Their example encourages readers to pursue good works and to recognize righteousness wherever it is sincerely practiced.

phrases.translation: They will never be denied the reward for any good they have done.
phrases.explanation: The good these people have done will not be denied to them. Their deeds are recognized by Allah, reinforcing the previous verses’ acknowledgment of upright individuals among the People of the Book. The passage rejects both prejudice and the idea that goodness goes unseen.

phrases.translation: And Allah has ˹perfect˺ knowledge of those mindful ˹of Him˺
phrases.explanation: Allah knows those who are mindful of Him. Divine knowledge encompasses sincere intentions and actions, including those that communities overlook. The verse reassures people who do good faithfully that their reward is not dependent on public recognition.

phrases.translation: Indeed, neither the wealth nor children of the disbelievers will be of any benefit to them against Allah.
phrases.explanation: For those who reject faith, wealth and children cannot protect them against Allah’s judgment. The verse does not condemn family or possessions themselves. It warns against relying on worldly status as a substitute for moral and spiritual responsibility.

phrases.translation: It is they who will be the residents of the Fire.
phrases.explanation: The verse describes the disbelievers under discussion as destined for the Fire. This is a warning about ultimate accountability, not authority for people to pronounce the fate of particular individuals. The following image explains how efforts without sound foundations may be lost.

phrases.translation: They will be there forever
phrases.explanation: They will remain there forever, the verse says. Its severe warning follows the chapter’s discussion of persistent rejection and judgment. Read the passage as a call to take faith seriously, while remembering that Allah alone knows each person’s final state.

phrases.translation: The good they do in this worldly life is like the harvest of an evil people struck by a bitter wind,
phrases.explanation: The verse compares the good done by the disbelievers in this worldly life to a harvest struck by a bitter wind. A crop may appear promising yet be destroyed before it can benefit its growers. The image emphasizes how vulnerable worldly effort is without a sound spiritual foundation.

phrases.translation: destroying it ˹completely˺.
phrases.explanation: The wind destroys the harvest completely, illustrating the loss of expected benefit. The verse follows a warning that wealth and children cannot serve as protection from Allah. It directs attention to the ultimate value and consequences of a person’s choices.

phrases.translation: Allah never wronged them,
phrases.explanation: Allah did not wrong the people described. Rather, they wronged themselves. The verse places responsibility for their loss on their own choices, not on injustice by Allah. This reinforces the assurance in verse 108 that Allah desires no injustice for creation.

phrases.translation: but they wronged themselves
phrases.explanation: Their own actions brought about the loss represented by the ruined harvest. The verse warns that outwardly good or successful efforts cannot erase persistent wrongdoing. Its point is accountability, not that every good deed by a non-Muslim is worthless in ordinary human terms.

phrases.translation: O believers!
phrases.explanation: The verse addresses believers directly before warning them about close confidants who would harm them. The warning is behavior-based: it concerns people who actively seek to cause harm, not everyone outside the Muslim community. The context asks for discernment, not indiscriminate suspicion.

phrases.translation: Do not associate closely with others who would not miss a chance to harm you.
phrases.explanation: Believers are cautioned against close association with people who would exploit the opportunity to injure them. The criterion is demonstrated hostile intent. It should not be expanded into a ban on friendship, cooperation, or fair dealings with people of other faiths.

phrases.translation: Their only desire is to see you suffer.
phrases.explanation: The hostile group is described as wanting believers to suffer. This motive explains why trust should be given thoughtfully. The verse addresses deliberate adversaries, not ordinary neighbors or colleagues who hold different beliefs.

phrases.translation: Their prejudice has become evident from what they say—
phrases.explanation: Their prejudice can already be heard in what they say, the verse notes. Speech provides evidence of intent, so believers should pay attention to actual conduct rather than assume hostility based only on identity. The next phrase contrasts spoken words with hidden feelings.

phrases.translation: and what their hearts hide is far worse. We have made Our revelations clear to you, if only you understood
phrases.explanation: What their hearts conceal is said to be worse, and the revelations make the warning clear. The closing urges discernment in response to real hostility. It does not encourage spying or hatred, but asks believers to protect themselves with awareness and sound judgment.

phrases.translation: Here you are! You love them but they do not love you,
phrases.explanation: The verse describes affection that is not returned by the particular hostile people in context. It does not claim that Muslims should distrust every person from another community. The warning concerns those whose actions reveal enmity despite courteous appearances.

phrases.translation: and you believe in all Scriptures.
phrases.explanation: Believers affirm all revealed Scriptures, while the people addressed are portrayed as not sharing that commitment toward them. The contrast is theological, but it does not erase the upright People of the Book acknowledged just above.

phrases.translation: When they meet you they say, “We believe.”
phrases.explanation: The hostile people say they believe when meeting the believers. The verse contrasts this public claim with their private anger, exposing hypocrisy in the specific group described. It asks readers to discern conduct carefully without assuming every polite statement is false.

phrases.translation: But when alone, they bite their fingertips in rage.
phrases.explanation: When alone, they bite their fingertips in rage, a vivid image of frustrated hostility. The action is figurative language that conveys intense resentment. The verse portrays a particular adversarial attitude rather than inviting believers to respond with hatred.

phrases.translation: Say, ˹O Prophet,˺ “˹May you˺ die of your rage!”
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told to answer with an emphatic rejoinder about their rage. In context, it exposes that their anger cannot undo the truth or control the believers. The phrase belongs to this charged exchange, not a general model for everyday speech.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah knows best what is ˹hidden˺ in the heart
phrases.explanation: Allah knows best what is hidden in the heart. This closes the warning by leaving hidden motives to divine knowledge. Believers may notice evidence of hostility, but only Allah has complete access to people’s inner thoughts and final accountability.

phrases.translation: When you ˹believers˺ are touched with good,
phrases.explanation: The verse says that the adversaries grieve when believers experience good fortune. This continues the description of specific hostile people introduced earlier. It does not suggest that every outsider resents Muslim success. The passage identifies a particular antagonistic response.

phrases.translation: they grieve; but when you are afflicted with evil,
phrases.explanation: When believers suffer hardship, the same adversaries rejoice. The contrast reveals their hostility through their reactions to others’ fortune and misfortune. The verse encourages awareness of such conduct while not projecting it onto people who have shown no enmity.

phrases.translation: they rejoice. ˹Yet,˺ if you are patient and mindful ˹of Allah˺, their schemes will not harm you in the least.
phrases.explanation: Patience and mindfulness of Allah prevent hostile schemes from ultimately defeating believers. This is spiritual reassurance, not a promise that believers will never face material harm. Their steadiness and ethical conduct matter even when circumstances are difficult.

phrases.translation: Surely Allah is Fully Aware of what they do
phrases.explanation: Allah is fully aware of what the adversaries do. The verse closes by placing both schemes and suffering within divine knowledge. Believers are encouraged to remain patient and mindful rather than imitate the hostility they encounter.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when you left your home in the early morning
phrases.explanation: The Prophet’s departure before daybreak recalls the preparations for the Battle of Uhud. He took practical steps to position the believers for the coming danger. The verse presents leadership as involving planning and care, while the next phrase reminds readers that Allah knows every action.

phrases.translation: to position the believers in the battlefield.
phrases.explanation: The believers are positioned in the battlefield, showing that faith does not mean neglecting preparation. The account is rooted in a particular historical encounter. It portrays the Prophet organizing the community while relying on Allah rather than treating strategy and trust as opposites.

phrases.translation: And Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing
phrases.explanation: Allah is All-Hearing and All-Knowing, aware of what people say and what they intend. The names reassure believers that their prayers and fears are known, even under pressure. They also remind leaders that hidden motives remain visible to Allah.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember˺ when two groups among you ˹believers˺ were about to cower,
phrases.explanation: Two groups among the believers nearly lost heart before the battle. The verse acknowledges fear honestly rather than pretending that faithful people never feel it. Its account helps readers see courage as something that can be renewed, not the absence of human vulnerability.

phrases.translation: then Allah reassured them.
phrases.explanation: Allah reassured the two groups, helping them recover their resolve. The verse attributes support to Allah without denying that the believers faced a real decision. Encouragement and spiritual trust helped them continue through an uncertain moment.

phrases.translation: So in Allah let the believers put their trust
phrases.explanation: Believers are told to place their trust in Allah. Trust does not mean refusing to prepare or feeling no fear. The preceding account includes both planning and anxiety. It means relying ultimately on Allah while acting responsibly.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Allah made you victorious at Badr
phrases.explanation: The verse recalls the earlier victory at Badr, where the believers faced a much larger force. That memory provides perspective after the preparations for Uhud. It reminds the community that numbers alone do not decide an outcome.

phrases.translation: when you were ˹vastly˺ outnumbered.
phrases.explanation: The believers were vastly outnumbered at Badr, yet Allah granted them victory. The verse calls them to mindfulness and gratitude rather than pride in success. Remembering help received can strengthen trust during later hardship.

phrases.translation: So be mindful of Allah, perhaps you will be grateful
phrases.explanation: Mindfulness of Allah is linked with gratitude. Victory is not presented as a reason for arrogance or as proof that every future encounter will have the same outcome. The verse asks believers to recognize support and remain faithful in response.

phrases.translation: ˹Remember, O Prophet,˺ when you said to the believers,
phrases.explanation: The Prophet recalls telling the believers about Allah’s promised help. The verse places this assurance within the pressure of battle, when people needed courage. It presents prophetic encouragement as a means of strengthening the community rather than glorifying military power.

phrases.translation: “Is it not enough that your Lord will send down a reinforcement of three thousand angels
phrases.explanation: The promised reinforcement is described as three thousand angels. In the verse, the promise serves to reassure the believers that Allah is able to support them. The number belongs to this particular account and is not a formula for guaranteeing victory in every conflict.

phrases.translation: for your aid?”
phrases.explanation: The angels are described as coming to aid the believers. The following verse conditions further reinforcement on steadfastness and mindfulness of Allah. Together, the passage connects divine support with perseverance, while verse 126 clarifies that victory ultimately comes from Allah.

phrases.translation: Most certainly, if you ˹believers˺ are firm and mindful ˹of Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The verse sets steadfastness and mindfulness of Allah as conditions in the scenario it describes. Courage here includes composure and obedience under pressure, not aggression or disregard for harm. The promise addresses the believers in a specific battle context.

phrases.translation: and the enemy launches a sudden attack on you, Allah will reinforce you with five thousand angels
phrases.explanation: If the enemy launches a sudden attack, the verse promises reinforcement by five thousand angels. This reassurance is part of the Qur’an’s account of the battle and its divine support. It should not be turned into a general guarantee that every faithful army will win.

phrases.translation: designated ˹for battle˺
phrases.explanation: The angels are described as designated for battle. This promise is framed by steadfastness and mindfulness, not simply by numerical superiority. It comforts the believers facing sudden danger, while the next verse clarifies that victory ultimately comes from Allah.

phrases.translation: Allah ordained this ˹reinforcement˺ only as good news for you
phrases.explanation: The reinforcement is described as good news for the believers. The announcement is meant to strengthen their hope and courage in a tense situation. It is not a spectacle for its own sake. Its purpose is to reassure those facing danger.

phrases.translation: and reassurance for your hearts.
phrases.explanation: The promise reassures the believers’ hearts. The verse recognizes that morale and confidence matter when a community is afraid. Spiritual reassurance does not deny the danger, but helps people face it with steadiness.

phrases.translation: And victory comes only from Allah—the Almighty, All-Wise—
phrases.explanation: Victory comes only from Allah, the Almighty and All-Wise. The angels are not independent sources of power. All help depends on Allah’s will and wisdom. The next verse describes the hoped-for outcome of the battle in continuation of this statement.

phrases.translation: to destroy a group of the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: The sentence continues by describing the destruction of a group of the disbelievers. This is tied to the battle context of the preceding verses, not a general command against people who hold another belief. The passage describes conflict between particular forces.

phrases.translation: and humble the rest, causing them to withdraw in disappointment
phrases.explanation: The remainder describes the opponents being humbled and withdrawing disappointed. This is a report of the battle’s outcome as framed by the Qur’an. Read with verse 128, it does not authorize the Prophet or believers to determine who Allah should punish or forgive.

phrases.translation: You ˹O Prophet˺ have no say in the matter.
phrases.explanation: The Prophet is told that he does not control the final outcome for his opponents. Even in conflict, ultimate judgment belongs to Allah. The verse restrains the desire for vengeance and reminds the Prophet that human beings cannot decide another person’s final fate.

phrases.translation: It is up to Allah to turn to them in mercy or punish them,
phrases.explanation: Allah may turn toward the wrongdoers in mercy or punish them. This leaves open the possibility of repentance and change, even after serious wrongdoing. The verse shifts judgment from human retaliation to Allah’s knowledge and justice.

phrases.translation: for indeed they are wrongdoers
phrases.explanation: They are called wrongdoers, but the decision about their outcome remains Allah’s. The verse balances moral clarity with humility about judgment. The next verse reinforces that all creation and all matters belong to Allah alone.

phrases.translation: To Allah ˹alone˺ belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.
phrases.explanation: Everything in the heavens and earth belongs to Allah. The statement grounds His authority over judgment and mercy in His ownership of all creation. No community or leader can claim independent power over the final outcome of human beings.

phrases.translation: He forgives whoever He wills,
phrases.explanation: Allah forgives whom He wills and punishes whom He wills. This places final judgment with Allah, who knows each person fully. It is a reason for humility, not permission for people to assume that they know whom Allah will forgive.

phrases.translation: and punishes whoever He wills. And Allah is All-Forgiving, Most Merciful
phrases.explanation: Allah is All-Forgiving and Most Merciful. The attributes of mercy follow the statement of judgment, preventing readers from imagining that punishment is Allah’s only response. The passage calls people to seek forgiveness while leaving final decisions to Him.

phrases.translation: O believers! Do not consume interest, multiplying it many times over.
phrases.explanation: Believers are forbidden to consume interest that compounds many times over. The warning addresses a practice that can make debts grow and burden those already in need. It calls for financial dealings rooted in fairness, though detailed rulings on modern transactions require careful legal analysis.

phrases.translation: And be mindful of Allah,
phrases.explanation: Mindfulness of Allah is joined to the prohibition, making financial conduct part of religious accountability. The verse asks believers to consider not only what is profitable but whether it is just. Ethical restraint is presented as a path to lasting prosperity.

phrases.translation: so you may prosper
phrases.explanation: The hope is that believers will prosper through obedience. The verse does not promise that avoiding interest guarantees immediate wealth. It defines prosperity more broadly through faith and just conduct. The next verses continue with accountability and obedience.

phrases.translation: Guard yourselves against the Fire prepared for the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: Believers are urged to guard themselves against the Fire prepared for those who disbelieve. The warning follows a prohibition on exploitative financial conduct, showing that moral choices have spiritual consequences. It calls for vigilance, not despair, as the next verse points toward obedience and mercy.

phrases.translation: Obey Allah and the Messenger,
phrases.explanation: The verse calls believers to obey Allah and the Messenger. In context, this includes heeding guidance about fair conduct, faith, and communal life. Obedience is not blind loyalty to human leaders, but following the revealed message delivered by the Prophet.

phrases.translation: so you may be shown mercy
phrases.explanation: The purpose is to receive mercy. The verse connects obedience with Allah’s compassion rather than with self-sufficiency or moral boasting. It prepares the reader for a description of those who seek forgiveness and cultivate generous, forgiving character.

phrases.translation: And hasten towards forgiveness from your Lord
phrases.explanation: Believers are urged to hasten toward forgiveness, meaning they should promptly turn back to Allah rather than delay repentance. The invitation comes after warnings about wrongdoing and obedience. It presents returning to Allah as an active response open to everyone.

phrases.translation: and a Paradise as vast as the heavens and the earth,
phrases.explanation: Paradise is described as vast as the heavens and earth, conveying abundance beyond ordinary human measure. Its promised breadth gives hope to those who seek Allah’s mercy. The verse associates this destination with mindfulness of Allah.

phrases.translation: prepared for those mindful ˹of Allah˺
phrases.explanation: The garden is prepared for those mindful of Allah. The next verses explain what such mindfulness looks like in daily life: generosity, control of anger, pardon, and sincere repentance. Taqwa is therefore shown through practical character, not only private belief.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who donate in prosperity and adversity,
phrases.explanation: The mindful give both when they have plenty and when resources are scarce. Generosity is not postponed until conditions are perfect. The verse values a steady willingness to share while leaving room for people to give according to their actual means.

phrases.translation: control their anger,
phrases.explanation: They restrain their anger rather than letting it dictate harmful words or actions. The verse does not require pretending that anger is never felt. It praises governing the response. This discipline can protect relationships and prevent injustice.

phrases.translation: and pardon others.
phrases.explanation: They pardon people who have wronged them, adding mercy to self-control. Forgiveness does not mean denying harm or abandoning necessary boundaries. The passage praises letting go of resentment when doing so is right and constructive.

phrases.translation: And Allah loves the good-doers
phrases.explanation: Allah loves those who do good. The verse gathers generosity, restraint, and pardon into a portrait of ihsan, excellence in conduct. These qualities are offered as practical signs of mindfulness and a route toward the forgiveness mentioned just before.

phrases.translation: ˹They are˺ those who, upon committing an evil deed or wronging themselves,
phrases.explanation: The mindful are not portrayed as people who never make mistakes. They may commit an evil deed or wrong themselves, but they remember Allah afterward. The verse gives a realistic account of moral failure while showing that it need not become a person’s permanent state.

phrases.translation: remember Allah and seek forgiveness
phrases.explanation: They remember Allah and ask forgiveness. This response combines awareness of wrongdoing with hope in divine mercy. Sincere repentance takes responsibility rather than shifting blame, and it opens a path to repair what can be repaired.

phrases.translation: and do not knowingly persist in sin—
phrases.explanation: They do not knowingly persist in sin. The emphasis is not on never stumbling, but on refusing to make wrongdoing a settled choice after recognizing it. The verse describes repentance as a genuine turning away from continued harm.

phrases.translation: and who forgives sins except Allah
phrases.explanation: The verse asks who can forgive sins except Allah, directing hope to the only One with ultimate authority to forgive. The question encourages return rather than despair. It also underscores that seeking forgiveness must accompany a sincere effort not to persist in wrongdoing.

phrases.translation: Their reward is forgiveness from their Lord
phrases.explanation: The reward of these people begins with forgiveness from their Lord. This follows the description of those who repent, mend their ways, and do good. The promise emphasizes that recovery after wrongdoing is possible through sincere return to Allah.

phrases.translation: and Gardens under which rivers flow,
phrases.explanation: Their reward includes gardens with rivers flowing beneath them, an image of lasting abundance and life. Paradise is described through language people can grasp, while its full reality exceeds worldly experience. The next phrase stresses the permanence of this reward.

phrases.translation: staying there forever.
phrases.explanation: They remain in the gardens forever. The lasting reward contrasts with fleeting worldly gain and offers hope to those who live righteously. The verse concludes by praising the quality of work that leads to such a reward.

phrases.translation: How excellent is the reward for those who work ˹righteousness˺
phrases.explanation: How excellent is the reward for those who work righteousness. The passage has connected good deeds with repentance, generosity, and mercy toward others. Righteousness is therefore active and relational, not merely a claim about one’s identity.

phrases.translation: Similar situations came to pass before you,
phrases.explanation: The verse reminds its audience that similar events happened to earlier peoples. Their experience can help later generations recognize patterns in human behavior and the consequences of rejecting guidance. History becomes a source of learning rather than mere background.

phrases.translation: so travel throughout the land
phrases.explanation: People are invited to travel and observe the traces of earlier communities. Encountering the places where they lived can make historical lessons more concrete. The invitation encourages reflection on evidence and consequences, not tourism without thought.

phrases.translation: and see the fate of the deniers
phrases.explanation: The fate of those who denied the truth is presented as a warning. The verse asks readers to learn from past outcomes before repeating destructive choices. The following verse summarizes the Qur’an’s purpose as insight, guidance, and a reminder.

phrases.translation: This is an insight to humanity—
phrases.explanation: The Qur’an is described as an insight for humanity. Its teachings help people see moral and spiritual realities more clearly. The verse presents the message as broadly relevant, not restricted to a single historical audience.

phrases.translation: a guide
phrases.explanation: It is also a guide, offering direction for those seeking to live in accordance with Allah’s will. Guidance requires engagement and response. It is not simply information received without reflection or action.

phrases.translation: and a lesson to the God-fearing
phrases.explanation: The Qur’an is a lesson for those mindful of Allah. The verse gathers its roles as insight, direction, and reminder. Its benefit is especially recognized by people willing to reflect and let the message shape their choices.

phrases.translation: Do not falter or grieve,
phrases.explanation: Believers are told not to collapse into despair after a setback. The surrounding passage recalls Uhud, where the community suffered losses. The instruction recognizes grief but calls the believers to recover their courage and continue faithfully.

phrases.translation: for you will have the upper hand,
phrases.explanation: The promise of having the upper hand is conditional on being true believers. It points to strength grounded in faith and steadfastness, not an assurance of uninterrupted military or political dominance. The next verse explains that victory and defeat alternate.

phrases.translation: if you are ˹true˺ believers
phrases.explanation: Belief is the condition attached to the promise. In context, this means remaining faithful after hardship and learning from mistakes. The verse encourages resilience without denying loss or claiming that believers will never face another defeat.

phrases.translation: If you have suffered injuries ˹at Uḥud˺,
phrases.explanation: The verse acknowledges the injuries believers suffered at Uhud. Their pain is not minimized or treated as evidence that Allah had abandoned them. The comparison that follows places this loss alongside an earlier defeat suffered by their opponents.

phrases.translation: they suffered similarly ˹at Badr˺.
phrases.explanation: The opponents had suffered similar injuries at Badr. The comparison shows that hardship does not fall on only one side and that one day’s result does not define the whole struggle. It prepares the image of changing fortunes among people.

phrases.translation: We alternate these days ˹of victory and defeat˺ among people
phrases.explanation: Allah alternates days of victory and defeat among people. The changing fortunes test communities and reveal how they respond to success and loss. The verse encourages learning and steadfastness rather than assuming that military outcomes alone measure moral worth.

phrases.translation: so that Allah may reveal the ˹true˺ believers, choose martyrs from among you—
phrases.explanation: The events reveal true believers and include the choosing of martyrs from among the community. The verse gives meaning to loss without treating suffering as something to seek. It acknowledges sacrifice while placing the battle within a larger moral test.

phrases.translation: and Allah does not like the wrongdoers—
phrases.explanation: Allah does not like wrongdoers. The clause sets a moral boundary on the passage’s account of battle and loss: wrongdoing is not made acceptable by victory. The following verses continue to describe how the community is tested and purified.

phrases.translation: and distinguish the ˹true˺ believers
phrases.explanation: This phrase continues the previous verse’s account of alternating victory and defeat. The events distinguish those whose faith remains steady under pressure. The passage treats hardship as a test of commitment, not as proof that Allah has abandoned the believers.

phrases.translation: and destroy the disbelievers
phrases.explanation: The verse also speaks of destroying the disbelievers, continuing the battle context of Uhud. It describes the fate of opponents in that specific conflict, not a command against people of another faith generally. The next verses explain that trials reveal how people respond.

phrases.translation: Do you think you will enter Paradise
phrases.explanation: The believers are asked whether they expect to enter Paradise without first being tested. The question connects the preceding battle with the broader demands of faith. It does not mean that people earn Paradise by suffering, but that commitment becomes visible in difficult times.

phrases.translation: without Allah proving which of you ˹truly˺ struggled ˹for His cause˺ and patiently endured
phrases.explanation: Allah will make clear who truly struggles and patiently endures. The verse calls for perseverance in doing what is right, not seeking violence or hardship for its own sake. Trials reveal sincerity through a person’s response, including steadfastness and moral restraint. The question challenges believers to examine their expectations after a difficult battle. Faith is not a guarantee of an easy path. The following verse recalls their earlier desire for martyrdom and the shock of encountering its reality.

phrases.translation: You certainly wished ˹for the opportunity˺ for martyrdom
phrases.explanation: The believers had previously wished for the opportunity to attain martyrdom. The verse recalls the distance between an aspiration expressed safely and the reality of facing death. It invites honest reflection on courage without encouraging anyone to seek death.

phrases.translation: before encountering it,
phrases.explanation: They had wished for martyrdom before they faced it directly. Now they have seen the danger with their own eyes. The verse gently exposes human overconfidence and asks believers to learn humility from the gap between intention and experience.

phrases.translation: now you have seen it with your own eyes
phrases.explanation: Having witnessed the battle, the believers can no longer imagine martyrdom only in the abstract. The verse acknowledges the emotional weight of what happened at Uhud. It encourages reflection and steadiness rather than shame for feeling fear.

phrases.translation: Muḥammad is no more than a messenger;
phrases.explanation: Muhammad is described as a messenger, not an immortal figure. The verse addresses the shock and confusion that could follow a report of his death during battle. It directs the community to ground its faith in Allah and revelation rather than in one person’s continued presence.

phrases.translation: other messengers have gone before him.
phrases.explanation: Other messengers had already passed away, so Muhammad’s mortality does not cancel his message. The reminder places him within the history of prophets. It comforts believers by distinguishing devotion to the Messenger from worship, which belongs to Allah.

phrases.translation: If he were to die or to be killed,
phrases.explanation: The question includes either natural death or being killed. The community is asked to consider whether either outcome would make it abandon faith. The verse addresses a real crisis of morale and calls believers to remain committed through loss.

phrases.translation: would you regress into disbelief?
phrases.explanation: Regressing into disbelief after the Messenger’s death would contradict the faith they had received. The rhetorical question challenges them to consider whether their belief depends only on his physical presence. His message remains after he is gone.

phrases.translation: Those who do so will not harm Allah whatsoever.
phrases.explanation: Those who turn away cannot harm Allah. Divine truth does not depend on human loyalty, and abandoning faith harms the person who does so rather than diminishing Allah. The verse then promises reward for those who remain grateful and steadfast.

phrases.translation: And Allah will reward those who are grateful
phrases.explanation: Allah will reward those who are grateful. Gratitude here includes remaining faithful and recognizing the guidance received, even in grief. The verse does not deny sorrow over the Prophet’s death, but prevents sorrow from becoming a reason to abandon the message.

phrases.translation: No soul can ever die without Allah’s Will at the destined time.
phrases.explanation: No soul dies except by Allah’s will at its appointed time. In the battle context, this comforts believers facing danger and discourages the belief that fear alone can control death. The verse speaks of divine knowledge without removing human responsibility for choices.

phrases.translation: Those who desire worldly gain,
phrases.explanation: People may pursue worldly gain, the verse says. Material aims are not automatically wrong, but the next phrase presents them as a choice about what a person seeks most. The passage encourages believers to consider the long-term consequences of their priorities.

phrases.translation: We will let them have it,
phrases.explanation: Those who desire worldly gain are allowed to receive it. The wording recognizes that worldly rewards may be obtained, but does not call them the highest or lasting good. The contrast with heavenly reward asks readers to reflect on what they ultimately value.

phrases.translation: and those who desire heavenly reward,
phrases.explanation: Others seek reward in the Hereafter, choosing an aim beyond immediate benefit. The verse does not require abandoning every worldly responsibility. It challenges believers to make Allah’s approval and lasting reward central to their intentions.

phrases.translation: We will grant it to them.
phrases.explanation: Allah grants heavenly reward to those who seek it. The distinction between worldly and eternal aims is about the direction of the heart and the life one chooses. The closing returns to gratitude as a fitting response to divine generosity.

phrases.translation: And We will reward those who are grateful
phrases.explanation: Allah will reward those who are grateful. Gratitude links recognition of Allah’s gifts with faithful action. In the context of Uhud, the verse reassures believers that life and death are in Allah’s hands, while choices and intentions still matter.

phrases.translation: ˹Imagine˺ how many devotees fought along with their prophets
phrases.explanation: The verse recalls many devoted people who struggled alongside earlier prophets. Their example shows that difficulty is not unique to Muhammad’s community. Faithful people across generations have faced opposition while remaining committed to their prophetic guidance.

phrases.translation: and never faltered despite whatever ˹losses˺ they suffered in the cause of Allah,
phrases.explanation: They endured losses in the cause of Allah. In context this describes earlier struggles, not a general invitation to violence. The emphasis of the verse is on their perseverance and refusal to abandon what they believed was right.

phrases.translation: nor did they weaken or give in!
phrases.explanation: Despite loss, they did not weaken or surrender their commitment. The verse praises resilience under hardship, not stubbornness in wrongdoing. Their example encourages believers to remain principled when facing setbacks and to keep acting with courage and discipline.

phrases.translation: Allah loves those who persevere
phrases.explanation: Allah loves those who persevere. The verse ties divine love to steadfastness through difficulty. This is especially meaningful after Uhud, where believers were recovering from a painful defeat and needed to learn how to continue faithfully.

phrases.translation: And all they said was, “Our Lord!
phrases.explanation: The devotees’ prayer begins by turning directly to their Lord. Their response to hardship is neither despair nor boasting, but humble supplication. The following requests show how they seek forgiveness, steadiness, and help to remain faithful.

phrases.translation: Forgive our sins and excesses,
phrases.explanation: They ask Allah to forgive their sins and excesses, taking responsibility for their own failings. This is a vital part of their prayer. They do not blame all hardship on others, but seek correction and mercy for themselves.

phrases.translation: make our steps firm,
phrases.explanation: They ask for firm steps, seeking steadiness when facing danger and uncertainty. The request is for moral and spiritual resolve as well as courage. It shows that perseverance depends on Allah’s support, not on self-confidence alone.

phrases.translation: and grant us victory over the disbelieving people.”
phrases.explanation: They ask Allah for victory over the disbelieving people confronting them. In this historical setting, the prayer concerns a specific conflict. Its sequence places the request after repentance and a plea for steadfastness, grounding victory in devotion rather than aggression.

phrases.translation: So Allah gave them the reward of this world
phrases.explanation: Allah granted them a reward in this world as well as in the Hereafter. The worldly reward may include support, honor, or relief, but the verse does not reduce divine favor to material success. It presents good conduct as valuable in both lives.

phrases.translation: and the excellent reward of the Hereafter.
phrases.explanation: Their reward in the Hereafter is excellent and lasting. The promise gives believers a horizon beyond immediate victory or defeat. It also reminds them that worldly outcomes alone cannot measure whether Allah is pleased with a person.

phrases.translation: For Allah loves the good-doers
phrases.explanation: Allah loves those who do good. The verse follows the devotees’ prayer and their perseverance, showing that faith is expressed through worship and conduct. Good-doing includes repentance, patience, and seeking justice without abandoning compassion.

phrases.translation: O believers!
phrases.explanation: The verse addresses believers directly before warning them about pressure from hostile opponents. The concern is that they might abandon their faith under influence or intimidation. This is not a command to hate or mistreat every person who disbelieves.

phrases.translation: If you yield to the disbelievers,
phrases.explanation: The warning concerns yielding to disbelievers who would pull the believers away from their faith. The surrounding passage describes a particular wartime confrontation. It should not be turned into a prohibition on peaceful friendship, cooperation, or fair treatment.

phrases.translation: they will drag you back to disbelief—
phrases.explanation: The danger named is a return to disbelief. The verse urges believers to hold to their convictions when facing pressure. Its focus is spiritual integrity, not physical conflict or a blanket judgment about all people outside the community.

phrases.translation: and you will become losers
phrases.explanation: Those who abandon their faith in this way will become losers, the verse warns. The loss is spiritual and ultimate. The next verse reassures believers that Allah, rather than their opponents, is their guardian and source of help.

phrases.translation: But no! Allah is your Guardian,
phrases.explanation: Allah is declared to be the believers’ guardian and protector. The verse answers the fear that hostile forces have the final power. Trust in Allah gives the community a source of support beyond political or military strength.

phrases.translation: and He is the best Helper
phrases.explanation: Allah is the best Helper. The claim encourages believers to seek divine support while still acting responsibly. It shifts attention away from dependence on opponents and prepares the next verse’s warning about associating partners with Allah.

phrases.translation: We will cast horror into the hearts of the disbelievers for associating ˹false gods˺ with Allah—
phrases.explanation: The verse describes horror being cast into the hearts of the disbelievers because of their association of false gods with Allah. It is framed in the battle context of Uhud and divine judgment. It is not a command for believers to terrorize people of another faith.

phrases.translation: a practice He has never authorized.
phrases.explanation: The practice is condemned because Allah never authorized associating false gods with Him. The verse presents the theological reason for the judgment it describes. It calls people to worship Allah alone, not to take revenge against individuals.

phrases.translation: The Fire will be their home—
phrases.explanation: The Fire is described as the wrongdoers’ home. This is a warning about the consequences of wrongdoing and false worship. The language is severe, but ultimate judgment belongs to Allah, not to human beings who encounter people with different beliefs.

phrases.translation: what an evil place for the wrongdoers to stay
phrases.explanation: The verse calls the Fire an evil place to stay. Its warning follows the chapter’s reminders of Allah’s power and judgment. Believers are urged to avoid wrongdoing themselves rather than use the passage as a reason to harm others.

phrases.translation: Indeed, Allah fulfilled His promise to you when you ˹initially˺ swept them away by His Will,
phrases.explanation: Allah had fulfilled His promise when the believers initially drove back the enemy at Uhud. The success is attributed to His will, not simply to military skill. The verse begins an honest account of how the situation later changed.

phrases.translation: then your courage weakened and you disputed about the command
phrases.explanation: The believers’ courage weakened and they disputed about the command. The passage does not hide the community’s lapse after early success. It invites reflection on how disagreement and loss of discipline can undo an advantage.

phrases.translation: and disobeyed, after Allah had brought victory within your reach.
phrases.explanation: The believers disobeyed after victory had seemed close. The setting is the setback at Uhud, traditionally associated with some archers leaving their position. The text’s broader point is that success brings tests and requires continued obedience.

phrases.translation: Some of you were after worldly gain
